大家好，既然我们已经讨论了虚拟机和管理程序，现在让我们进入实践环节。

虚拟机实际上需要什么才能运行良好且安全？

在本讲座中，我们将聚焦于四个要素：安全考量、网络配置、存储分配和资源管理。

这些决策决定了你的虚拟机是一个可靠的工具，还是一个缓慢、不安全且在关键时刻崩溃的烂摊子。

第一个安全问题是：这台虚拟机是用来做什么的？

培训实验室用的虚拟机与处理业务数据的虚拟机具有不同的风险。

工作负载越敏感，你就越需要对其进行加固。

包括强身份验证、补丁更新、最小化服务以及谨慎的网络配置。

虚拟机可以减小爆炸半径，但前提是你设计时考虑了隔离性和策略。

虚拟机的一个关键需求是定义边界。

它可以访问哪些网络，可以到达哪些文件共享，以及可以直通哪些设备。

像共享文件夹、共享剪贴板和USB直通这样的便利功能可能很有用，但它们也在客户机和主机之间创建了通道。在安全环境中，你要限制这些通道，因为隔离本身就是你最初进行虚拟化的主要原因之一。

网络配置决定了虚拟机如何通信。

最常见的选择是网络地址转换、桥接网络和仅主机模式。

网络地址转换适合在提供互联网访问的同时，让虚拟机对你的局域网保持隐藏。

桥接模式使虚拟机作为一台完整的设备出现在局域网上，拥有自己的网络存在。

仅主机模式允许主机和客户机之间进行通信，而不会暴露到更广泛的网络中。

选择正确的模式是虚拟机设计的核心要求。

当你想要安全的出站访问而不直接暴露虚拟机时，请使用网络地址转换。

当虚拟机需要像服务器一样被访问，或者需要正常加入局域网时，请使用桥接模式。

当你构建隔离的实验室或处理有风险的测试时，请使用仅主机模式。

在IT工作中，正确的网络模式可以防止许多问题，包括测试系统意外暴露给生产网络。

虚拟机存储不仅仅关乎磁盘有多大，还关乎性能和增长。

如果虚拟磁盘太小，操作系统就会耗尽空间并变得不稳定。

如果存储太慢，即使中央处理器和内存没问题，一切也会感觉像是坏了。

你还需要考虑是想要精简配置、按需增长的磁盘，还是为了可预测的性能而使用固定大小的磁盘。

不同的工作负载对存储的压力不同。

执行轻度办公任务的虚拟机使用适度的磁盘性能即可，但数据库虚拟机或构建服务器虚拟机则需要快速存储。

对于许多环境来说，基于固态驱动器的存储是区分虚拟机表现优异还是令人痛苦的关键。

因此，一项要求是使存储性能与工作负载相匹配，而不仅仅是匹配磁盘大小。

中央处理器分配是关于给予虚拟机足够的处理能力以保持响应，同时不让主机资源枯竭。一个常见的初学者错误是分配过多的虚拟中央处理器，这实际上会因调度开销而降低性能。

良好的做法是从适度的配置开始，测量性能，然后再扩展。

虚拟机共享资源，所以你的设计需要平衡。

内存通常是虚拟化中的第一个限制性资源。

如果你在多个虚拟机之间过度分配内存，主机可能会变得不稳定或开始交换，这会彻底破坏性能。

如果你给虚拟机分配的内存不足，客户机操作系统就会发生抖动并感觉无法使用。

因此，内存规划是最重要的虚拟机需求之一。

给予客户机工作负载足够的内存，但要为主机和其他虚拟机保留足够的内存。在操作上，虚拟机需要一个恢复计划。

快照在进行更新或高风险更改之前非常有用，但它们不是完整的备份策略。

备份可以防范磁盘故障、损坏、勒索软件和人为错误。

一个运行良好的虚拟机环境会使用快照进行短期回滚，并使用备份进行长期恢复。

虚拟机仍然需要维护，包括补丁更新、防病毒或端点保护（视情况而定）、日志审查和性能监控。

你需要监控中央处理器、内存、磁盘输入输出和网络使用情况，以便在用户抱怨之前发现瓶颈。

虚拟机环境可能会隐藏问题，因为所有东西都是共享的。

所以，监控能告诉你哪个资源实际上是问题所在。

在部署之前，请确认虚拟机的用途和安全边界、正确的网络模式、带有增长计划的充足存储、合理的中央处理器和内存分配以及备份方法。

还要确认你启用的任何集成功能，如共享文件夹、剪贴板、USB，是否确实是必需的。

最好的虚拟机是枯燥、稳定、可预测且易于恢复的。

这就是虚拟机的需求。

要构建可靠的虚拟机，你首先要规划安全，有意地配置网络，根据容量和性能分配存储，并管理中央处理器和内存以保持主机健康。

然后你添加恢复措施，即快照加备份以及持续监控，这样问题就不会悄悄找上门来。

接下来，我们可以将这些需求应用到真实的实验室设计、故障排除场景或考试风格的问题中，具体取决于你想练习什么。

英文原文

Hey everyone,now that we have talked about VMs and hypervisors,let's get practical.

What does a VM actually need to run well and safely?

In this lecture,we'll focus on four essentials,security considerations,network configuration,storage allocation,and resource management.

These decisions determine whether your VM is a reliable tool or a slow insecure mess that breaks at the worst time.

The first security question is what is this VM for?

A training lab VM has different risk than a VM that processes business data.

The more sensitive the workload,the more you harden it.

Strong authentication,patching,minimal services and careful networking.

VMs can reduce BLAST radius but only if you design them with isolation and policy in mind.

A key VM requirement is defining boundaries.

What networks can it access,what file shares can it reach and what devices can be passed through.

Convenience features like shared folders,shared tripboard and USB pass-through can be useful,but they also create pathways between guest and host.In secure environments,you limit those pathways because isolation is one of the main reasons you virtualize in the first place.

Network configuration determines how the VM communicates.

The most common choices are NAT,bridge networking and host only.

NAT is good for giving internet access while keeping the VM hidden from your LAN.

Bridged makes the VM appear as a full device on the LAN with its own network presence.

Host only allows communication between host and guest without broader network exposure.

Choosing the right mode is a core VM design requirement.

Use NAT when you want safe outbound access without exposing the VM directly.

Use bridged when the VM needs to be reachable like a server or needs to join the LAN normally.

Use host only when you're building an isolated lab or dealing with risky testing.

In IT work,the right network mode prevents a lot of problems including accidental exposure of test systems to production networks.

VM storage isn't just how big is the disk,it's also about performance and growth.

If the virtual disk is too small,the OS runs out of space and becomes unstable.

If storage is too slow,everything feels broken even if CPU and RAM are fine.

You also think about whether you want thin provisioning,grow on demand disks or fixed size disks for predictable performance.

Different workloads stress storage differently.

A VM doing light office tasks is fine with modest disk performance,but a database VM or a build server VM needs fast storage.

For many environments,SSD backed storage is the difference between VMs are great and VMs are painful.

So one requirement is matching storage performance to workload,not just matching disk size.

CPU allocation is about giving the VM enough processing to stay responsive without starving the host.A common beginner mistake is assigning too many virtual CPUs which can actually reduce performance due to scheduling overhead.

Good practice is to start modestly,measure performance,then scale up.

VMs share resources so your design needs balance.

RAM is usually the first limiting resource in virtualization.

If you over allocate RAM across multiple VMs,the host can become unstable or start swapping,which destroys performance.

If you under allocate RAM to a VM,the guest OS thrashes and feels unusable.

So RAM planning is one of the most important VM requirements.

Give enough for the guest workload,but keep enough for the host and other VMs.Operationally,a VM needs a recovery plan.

Snapshots are great before updates or risky changes,but they aren't a full backup strategy.

Backups protect against disk failures,corruption,ransomware and human mistakes.

A well-run VM environment uses snapshots for short-term rollback and backups for long-term recovery.

VMs still need maintenance,patching,antivirus or endpoint protection where appropriate,log review,and performance monitoring.

You monitor CPU,RAM,disk input and output,and network usage so you can spot bottlenecks before users complain.

VM environments can hide problems because everything shares everything.

So monitoring is what tells you which resource is actually the problem.

Before you deploy,confirm the VM's purpose and security boundaries,the correct network mode,enough storage with a growth plan,sensible CPU and RAM allocations and a backup approach.

Also confirm that any integration features you enable shared folders,clipboard,USB are truly needed.

The best VMs are boring,stable,predictable and easy to recover.

That's VM requirements.

To build reliable VMs,you plan security first,configure networking intentionally,allocate storage based on both capacity and performance,and manage CPU and RAM so the host stays healthy.

Then you add recovery,snapshots plus backups and continuous monitoring so issues don't sneak up on you.

Next,we can apply these requirements to real lab designs,troubleshooting scenarios or exam style questions depending on what you want to practice.

187. 云服务模型概述

大家好，今天我们将以一个非常简单的问题开始云计算的学习。

当你使用云时，你实际上购买的是什么？

云服务模型解释了你自己要做多少工作，以及云提供商为你做多少工作。

三大模型是基础设施即服务、平台即服务和软件即服务，你在现代信息技术中会到处听到它们。

可以把它们想象成三个级别的帮助。

一个提供原始的构建模块，一个提供用于构建应用程序的现成平台，还有一个提供你只需登录即可使用的成品软件。

一旦你理解了这三种模型，选择服务和排除故障就会变得容易得多。

理解云模型的最佳方式是关注责任。

谁负责设置，谁负责维护，以及当出现问题时谁负责修复。

在一种模型中，你可能需要负责选择操作系统、安装更新以及配置安全设置。

在另一种模型中，提供商处理大部分技术底层工作，而你主要专注于用户、设置和你的数据。

随着你从更多的控制权转向更多的便利性，你通常是用灵活性来换取简单性。

这就是为什么云不仅仅是使用别人的计算机。

它是选择你想要保留多少管理工作。

如果你总是问这项任务归谁管，你就能做出更明智的云决策。

基础设施即服务是最接近传统信息的模型，只不过是租用而不是拥有。

你获得虚拟计算机、存储和网络，然后在此基础上构建你的环境。

你选择自己的操作系统，安装自己的应用程序，并决定如何保护和修补它们。

当你需要灵活性、特殊配置，或者将旧系统迁移到云端时，这非常棒。

代价是你仍然需要做大量的动手工作，只是不需要购买物理硬件而已。

人们通常在选择最大控制权且不介意管理工作量时选择此模型。

基础设施即服务常用于提升和转移迁移，即组织以最小的重新设计将现有服务器迁移到云端。

它也用于测试环境、临时项目服务器以及需要特定操作系统设置的工作负载。

许多信息技术团队在需要自定义网络布局、专用安全工具或不适合托管平台的特殊软件时使用基础设施即服务。

当你希望通过快速添加更多服务器来扩展规模，而不是等待硬件采购时，它也很有用。

关键点在于，基础设施即服务很灵活，但它期望你表现得像一名服务器管理员。

如果你的团队能很好地管理服务器，基础设施即服务是一个强有力的起点。

平台即服务旨在减少服务器工作，以便你可以专注于更快地构建应用程序。

你无需担心操作系统和服务器补丁，而是将应用程序部署到一个已经知道如何运行它的平台上。

该平台可以处理许多幕后任务，如扩展、健康检查和更新运行时环境。

这在开发团队中很受欢迎，因为它减少了设置时间并消除了许多例行维护工作。

你仍然负有责任，特别是围绕你的应用程序代码、设置和数据，但平台处理了大部分基础设施。

如果你想要速度和一致性，平台即服务可以成为一个很好的中间地带。

平台即服务常用于网络应用程序、应用程序接口、移动后端以及需要快速部署和平滑扩展的内部业务应用程序。

对于实践持续交付等现代开发方法的团队来说，它也很受欢迎，因为频繁更新是常态。

当你想要标准化环境，从而使“在我的机器上能运行”不再成为问题时，平台即服务会有所帮助。

许多组织为新应用程序选择平台即服务，因为它减少了他们必须进行的基础设施规划工作量。

代价是，与基础设施即服务相比，你在自定义底层环境方面的自由度可能较小。

作为交换，你通常会获得更快的开发速度和更少的运营开销。

软件即服务是最简单的模型，因为你使用的是已经构建完成的完整产品。

你通常只需打开浏览器或应用程序，登录并开始工作。

提供商负责基础设施、应用程序更新以及大部分幕后的技术维护。

你的责任通常在于管理账户、权限、设置以及数据的使用和共享方式。

这种模型在电子邮件、协作工具、客户管理系统和许多日常业务功能中极为常见。

软件即服务之所以流行，是因为它让公司能够快速获得价值，而无需构建或管理平台。

代价是你通常获得的自定义程度不如基础设施即服务或平台即服务。

软件即服务通常被选用于标准业务需求，如电子邮件、文件共享、团队协作工具、人力资源系统和客户关系管理平台。当公司希望快速向数百或数千名用户推出工具时，它尤其有用。

当业务功能足够普遍，以至于已经存在设计良好的产品时，软件即服务效果很好。

该模型减少了在内部运行服务器的需求，并减少了补丁和升级的工作量。

挑战在于，你需要良好的用户管理、强大的访问控制以及明确的数据共享策略。

换句话说，软件即服务减少了技术基础设施工作，但增加了治理和账户安全的重要性。

现在让我们谈谈所有三种模型的主要权衡：控制权与便利性。

拥有更多的控制权，你可以进行更多的自定义，但你也有更多的东西需要维护，并且有更多的方法可能导致配置错误。

拥有更多的便利性，事情更容易使用，但你在深入更改系统方面可能会受到限制。

正确的模型取决于你想要做什么、你的团队技能如何以及你需要多快看到结果。

一些组织为不同的项目选择不同的模型，因为没有一种模型适合所有情况。

良好的云策略通常是混合的，而不是单一的选择。

明智的做法是选择既能满足实际需求又最简单的模型。

一个常见的误解是认为云提供商会自动处理所有安全问题，事实并非如此。

在每种模型中，提供商处理某些层，而你处理其他层。

例如，即使提供商运行数据中心和硬件，你可能仍然需要负责账户安全、访问权限以及保护你的数据。

你选择的模型会改变你所做的技术安全工作量，但永远不会将你的责任降为零。

这就是为什么身份管理、强密码和多因素认证在云环境中如此重要。

理解共同责任可以防止推诿扯皮，并帮助你设计更安全的系统。如果你知道自己拥有什么，你就知道要保护什么以及监控什么。

当你选择云模型时，首先问问自己实际上需要控制什么。

如果你必须为专用应用程序控制操作系统和环境，你很可能会倾向于基础设施即服务。

如果你的主要目标是快速部署应用程序而无需担心服务器，平台即服务通常是更好的选择。

如果你只需要一个工具来完成业务工作，且自定义不是优先事项，软件即服务往往是最佳选项。

还要考虑人员配备。

你有能够管理服务器的人员吗，还是你想减少那部分工作量？

成本不仅仅关乎价格，还关乎时间和技能。

一个能节省管理员时间的模型，即使订阅价格看起来更高，总体上也可能是更便宜的。

在真实的组织中，同时使用所有三种云模型是非常正常的。

一家公司可能会使用软件即服务来处理电子邮件和协作，使用平台即服务进行新应用程序开发，并使用基础设施即服务来处理不适合其他任何地方的遗留系统。

这种混合发生是因为不同的工作负载有不同的需求，而云足够灵活以支持这一点。

诀窍是要有意识地去做，以免环境变成随机服务的混乱混合体。

良好的文档、清晰的所有权和一致的安全实践能让事情保持可控。

如果你清楚地理解这三种模型，你就可以向技术和非技术团队解释这些选择。这在信息技术领域是一个巨大的职业优势。

做得好。

今天你学习了三大云服务模型以及它们在现实生活中的感受。

基础设施即服务给你最多的控制权，感觉就像在管理服务器，而平台即服务专注于运行你的代码而无需繁重的服务器工作，软件即服务则为你提供即用型应用程序，由提供商处理大部分维护工作。

主要的决定始终是你需要多少控制权，以及你想要承担多少管理工作。

如果你不断追问谁来做这项工作，你几乎总是能为这项工作选择正确的模型。

接下来，我们将从服务模型转向部署模型，谈谈私有云，即具有云风格的好处，但专为单一组织构建。

英文原文

Hey everyone,today we are starting cloud computing with a very simple question.

When you use the cloud,what are you actually buying?

Cloud service models explain how much work you do yourself versus how much work the cloud provider does for you.

The three big models are IAAS,PAAS and SAAS and you'll hear them everywhere in modern IT.

Think of them like three levels of help.

One gives you raw building blocks,one gives you a ready platform for building apps and one gives you finished software you just log into.

Once you understand these three models,picking services and troubleshooting problems gets a lot easier.

The best way to understand cloud models is to focus on responsibility.

Who sets things up,who maintains it,and who fixes it when something breaks.

In one model,you might be responsible for choosing an operating system,installing updates,and configuring security settings.

In another model,the provider handles most of the technical plumbing and you mainly focus on users,settings and your data.

As you move from more control to more convenience,you usually trade flexibility for simplicity.

This is why cloud is not just using someone else's computer.

It's choosing how much management you want to keep.

If you always ask who owns this task,you'll make smarter cloud decisions.

Infrastructure as a service is the model that feels most like traditional IT,just rented instead of owned.

You get virtual computers,storage and networking,and then you build your environment on top of that.

You choose your operating system,you install your applications,and you decide how to secure and patch them.

This is great when you need flexibility,special configurations,or you're moving an older system into the cloud.

The trade-off is that you're still doing a lot of hands-on work just without buying physical hardware.

People often pick this model when they want maximum control and don't mind the management workload.

IAAS is commonly used for lift and shift migrations,where an organization moves an existing server into the cloud with minimal redesign.

It's also used for test environments,temporary project servers,and workloads that need specific operating system settings.

Many IT teams use IAAS when they need custom network layouts,special security tools or unusual software that doesn't fit into a managed platform.

It's also useful when you want to scale up by adding more servers quickly rather than waiting for hardware purchases.

The key point is that IAAS is flexible,but it expects you to act like a server admin.

If your team can manage servers well,IAAS is a strong starting point.

Platform as a service is designed to reduce the server work so you can focus on building applications faster.

Instead of worrying about operating systems and server patching,you deploy your application to a platform that already knows how to run it.

The platform can handle many behind the scenes tasks like scaling,health checks and updating the runtime environment.

This is popular with development teams because it reduces setup time and removes a lot of routine maintenance.

You still have responsibilities especially around your application code,your settings and your data,but the platform handles much of the infrastructure.

If you want speed and consistency,PaaS can be a great middle ground.

PaaS is often used for web applications,APIs,mobile backends,and internal business apps that need to deploy quickly and scale smoothly.

It's also popular for teams practicing modern development methods like continuous delivery where frequent updates are normal.

PaaS can help when you want standardized environments so that it works on my machine doesn't become a problem.

Many organizations choose PaaS for new applications because it reduces the amount of infrastructure planning they have to do.

The trade-off is that you may have less freedom to customize the underlying environment compared to IAS.

In exchange,you usually gain faster development and less operations overhead.

Software as a service is the simplest model because you are using a complete product that is already built.

You usually open a browser or an app,sign in and start working.

The provider handles the infrastructure,the application updates and most of the technical maintenance behind the scenes.

Your responsibilities are usually about managing accounts,permissions,settings and how data is used and shared.

This model is extremely common for email,collaboration tools,customer management systems and many everyday business functions.

SAS is popular because it lets companies get value quickly without building or managing a platform.

The trade-off is that you typically get less customization than you would with IAAS or PAAS.

SAS is often chosen for standard business needs like email,file sharing,teamwork tools,HR systems and CRM platforms.It's especially useful when a company wants to roll out a tool to hundreds or thousands of users quickly.

SAS works well when the business function is common enough that a well-designed product already exists.

This model reduces the need for running servers in-house and reduces the workload of patching and upgrades.

The challenge is that you need good user management,strong access controls and clear policies for data sharing.

In other words,SAS reduces technical infrastructure work but increases the importance of governance and account security.

Now let's talk about the main trade-off across all three models control versus convenience.

With more control,you can customize more,but you also have more things to maintain and more ways to misconfigure something.

With more convenience,things are easier to use,but you may have limits on how deeply you can change the system.

The right model depends on what you're trying to do,how skilled your team is,and how fast you need results.

Some organizations pick different models for different projects because no single model fits everything.

A good cloud strategy is usually a mix,not a single choice.

The smart move is selecting the simplest model that still meets the real requirements.

A common misconception is thinking the cloud provider handles all security automatically,and that's not how it works.

In every model,the provider handles certain layers and you handle other layers.

For example,even if the provider runs the data center and hardware,you may still be responsible for account security,access permissions,and protecting your data.

The model you choose changes how much technical security work you do,but it never reduces your responsibility to zero.

This is why identity management,strong passwords,and multi-factor authentication matter so much in cloud environments.

Understanding shared responsibility prevents blame games and helps you design safer systems.If you know what you own,you know what to secure and what to monitor.

When you're choosing a cloud model,start by asking what you actually need to control.

If you must control the operating system and the environment for a specialized application,you'll likely lean toward infrastructure as a service.

If your main goal is deploying an application quickly without worrying about servers,platform as a service is usually a better fit.

If you just need a tool to do a business job and customization is not the priority,software as a service is often the best option.

Also think about staffing.

Do you have people who can manage servers or do you want to reduce that workload?

Cost isn't just about pricing,it's also about time and skills.

A model that saves admin time can be cheaper overall even if the subscription price looks higher.

In real organizations,it's very normal to use all three cloud models at the same time.

A company might use software as a service for email and collaboration,platform as a service for new app development,and infrastructure as a service for legacy systems that don't fit neatly anywhere else.

This mix happens because different workloads have different needs,and cloud is flexible enough to support that.

The trick is being intentional so the environment doesn't turn into a messy mix of random services.

Good documentation,clear ownership,and consistent security practices keep things manageable.

If you understand the three models clearly,you can explain choices to both technical and non-technical teams.That's a big career advantage in IT.

Great job.

Today you learn the three major cloud service models and what they feel like in real life.

Infrastructure as a service gives you the most control and feels like managing servers,while platform as a service focuses on running your code without heavy server work,and software as a service gives you ready to use applications with the provider handling most maintenance.

The main decision is always how much control you need and how much management work you want to own.

If you keep asking who does the work,you'll almost always pick the right model for the job.

Next up,we'll shift from service models to deployment models by talking about private cloud,cloud style benefits,but built for just one organization.

189. 公有云

大家好，今天我们要讨论的是公有云，也就是大多数人提到“云”时所指的内容。

公有云是一种共享的云环境，由提供商构建大规模数据中心，并将其中的部分资源租给客户。

主要提供商包括亚马逊云科技、微软Azure和谷歌云，它们提供从虚拟机到数据库再到存储的各种服务。

其核心理念是你不需要购买硬件。

你按需租用，并随用随付。

这种模式之所以流行，是因为它快速、灵活且在全球范围内可用。

只要你能使用互联网连接，通常就能使用公有云。

有一件事让人们感到困惑，那就是共享基础设施。

共享并不意味着每个人都能看到其他人的数据。

它意味着物理硬件由许多客户共享，而每个客户都是隔离的。

可以把它想象成一栋公寓楼：大楼是共享的，但公寓是私人的。

公有云提供商在隔离和访问控制方面投入巨资，以确保一个租户无法访问另一个租户的资源。

整个模式之所以可行，是因为共享降低了成本，而隔离保障了客户的安全。

你仍然负有责任，比如正确配置权限，但共享部分关乎的是硬件效率。

这就是提供商能够以比大多数公司独自构建更低的成本提供巨大容量的原因。

亚马逊云科技是早期的领导者，以其庞大的服务目录和全球覆盖范围而闻名。

Azure在已经使用微软工具（如Windows Server和Microsoft 365）的组织中非常受欢迎，并且与企业身份系统紧密集成。

谷歌云通常在数据、分析和人工智能方面的优势被强调，并在技术密集型环境中得到广泛应用。

在实践中，这三家提供商都极具能力，而且许多技能可以在它们之间通用。

公司通常根据现有合同、员工经验以及哪些服务符合其需求来进行选择。

重要的一点是，公有云是一个生态系统，而不仅仅是租用一台服务器。

公有云之所以爆发式增长，是因为它消除了信息技术中最缓慢的部分：等待。

你无需规划采购、订购设备和安装硬件，而是可以在几分钟内配置资源。

这种速度改变了企业的运营方式，因为实验变得更便宜、更快。

公有云还使得在全球范围内启动业务变得更加容易，而无需构建全球数据中心。

它支持快速增长，这就是初创公司喜欢它的原因；但它也支持快速现代化，这也是企业使用它的原因。

在许多方面，公有云将基础设施变成了你可以按需请求的东西。

这种转变使信息技术更加敏捷且更具可扩展性。

公有云降低了前期成本，因为你无需先购买基础设施，这可能是一个巨大的商业优势。

你为所使用的资源付费，这可以减少容量浪费，特别是对于变化很大的工作负载。

然而，你必须管理你的使用情况，因为如果资源全天候运行，微小的成本也会累积起来。

云成本管理成为一项独立的技能，包括跟踪使用情况、关闭未使用的资源以及为工作负载选择合适的规模。

公有云通常将资本支出转化为运营支出，这是许多组织所偏好的。

好处是灵活性，但如果治理薄弱，风险就是意外的账单。

公有云常用于网络托管、应用程序后端、开发和测试环境、备份以及灾难恢复。

它还用于数据处理、分析和现代应用程序架构，在这些场景中，你希望使用可扩展的服务而不是管理服务器。

另一个主要用例是突发工作负载，即你需要临时额外容量的时候，比如销售活动或季节性需求。

当工作负载需求不可预测或速度至关重要时，公有云是一个合适的选择。

当你希望访问托管服务（如托管数据库和消息系统）时，它也很有用。简而言之，当你想要速度、规模和多样化的服务时，公有云表现出色。

公有云最显著的优势之一是弹性。

你可以在需求激增时扩展，在需求下降时缩减。

如果你设计了系统来实现这一点，这可以自动发生，从而有助于性能和成本。在传统数据中心，扩展可能意味着购买服务器并等待数周。

在公有云中，扩展通常只是一个配置选择和几次点击。

这改变了你设计应用程序的方式，因为你可以规划增长，而无需在第一天就购买最大容量。

它还有助于提高可靠性，因为你可以将工作负载分散到多个资源上。

弹性是公有云成为现代互联网服务默认选择的原因之一。

公有云提供商在许多地理区域拥有数据中心，这使得更容易服务于靠近客户居住地的用户。

这提高了性能，因为距离会影响延迟，尤其是对于实时应用程序。

全球基础设施还支持弹性，因为你可以构建在多个位置运行以抵御故障的系统。

即使你只在一个区域运行，通常也可以在该区域内设计冗余。

这对大多数公司来说，独自完成要困难得多。

全球覆盖是公有云最悄然强大的功能之一。

它既有助于性能，也有助于业务连续性。

公有云可以非常安全，但它要求正确的配置。

提供商负责底层基础设施的安全，但客户仍然控制对其资源的访问。

身份和访问管理变得至关重要，因为许多云事件源于权限过宽的账户或暴露的服务。

日志记录、监控和强身份验证实践非常重要，因为云环境变化迅速。

另一个关键是数据保护。

加密和备份应该经过规划，而不是想当然。

公有云安全是提供商控制与客户选择之间的合作伙伴关系。

如果你的访问控制马虎，云也无法挽救你。

公有云不仅仅是虚拟机，它是一个托管服务的生态系统。

托管数据库、对象存储、监控服务、无服务器函数和人工智能工具是常见的构建模块。

这些服务减少了你自己运行一切的需求，并且可以加快开发速度。

代价是你需要学习特定于提供商的服务，这可能会产生一定的依赖性。

许多组织接受这一点，因为生产力的提升是实实在在的。

公有云往往关乎明智地使用托管服务，而不是从头开始重建一切。

你越依赖托管服务，花在例行基础设施工作上的时间就越少。

公有云有一些缺点，你应该提前了解。

如果资源保持运行状态或不了解数据传输模式，可能会出现成本意外。

如果你围绕一家提供商的专用服务进行大量构建，可能会出现供应商锁定。

如果团队在没有标准或文档的情况下创建资源，治理可能会变得困难。

网络依赖性也很重要。

如果你的连接质量差，用户体验就会受到影响。

而且像任何环境一样，配置错误可能会引发安全问题。

好消息是，通过良好的规划，这些挑战是可以管理的。

当你将公有云视为一个经过工程设计的環境，而不是一个神奇的公用事业时，它的效果最好。

公有云非常适合小型组织，因为它避免了大量的前期采购，并允许快速成长。

它也非常适合大型组织，因为它支持全球部署、快速实验和现代化项目。

区别在于治理的规模。

较大的组织需要更强的策略、更严格的访问控制设计和更好的成本跟踪。

小型组织可以快速行动，但仍需要基本的纪律，以免成本和安全性失控。

无论哪种情况，公有云提供的灵活性都是传统数据中心难以匹敌的。

关键是将云的使用与真实的业务需求和实际的运营成熟度对齐。

公有云很强大，但它奖励良好的规划。

做得好。

公有云是由亚马逊云科技、Azure和谷歌云等公司提供的共享基础设施，旨在实现速度、全球覆盖和随用随付的灵活性。

它让你能够快速配置资源、向上和向下扩展，并访问庞大的托管服务生态系统。

你保留的主要责任是配置、访问控制以及管理你的使用情况，以保持成本可预测。

主要风险是如果团队缺乏协调，会出现成本意外、配置错误和治理问题。

既然你已经了解了私有云和公有云，下一步就是将它们结合起来。

接下来，我们将讨论混合云，即组织混合使用私有和公共环境，以为每种工作负载获得最佳匹配。

英文原文

Hey everyone,today we are talking public cloud,which is what most people mean when they say the cloud.

Public cloud is a shared cloud environment where a provider builds massive data centers and rents pieces of them to customers.

Major providers include AWS,Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud,and they offer everything from virtual machines to databases to storage.

The big idea is that you don't buy hardware.

You rent what you need and pay for it as you go.

This model is popular because it's fast,flexible and available globally.

If you can use an internet connection,you can usually use public cloud.

One thing that confuses people is shared infrastructure.

Shared does not mean everyone sees everyone's data.

It means the physical hardware is shared across many customers while each customer is isolated.

Think of it like an apartment building,shared building,private apartments.

Public cloud providers invest heavily in separation and access controls so one tenant cannot access another tenant's resources.

The whole model works because sharing drives costs down while isolation keeps customers safe.

You still have responsibilities like configuring permissions correctly but the shared part is about hardware efficiency.

This is how providers can offer huge capacity at lower cost than most companies can build alone.

AWS was the early leader and is known for having a huge catalog of services and global reach.

Azure is very popular in organizations that already use Microsoft tools like Windows Server and Microsoft 365 and it integrates tightly with enterprise identity systems.

Google Cloud is often highlighted for strengths in data,analytics and AI and it's widely used in tech heavy environments.

In practice,all three providers are extremely capable and many skills transfer between them.

Companies often choose based on existing contracts,staff experience and which services fit their needs.

The important point is that public cloud is an ecosystem,not just renting a server.

Public cloud exploded because it removed the slowest part of IT,waiting.

Instead of planning purchases,ordering equipment and installing hardware,you can provision resources in minutes.

That speed changes how businesses operate because experimentation becomes cheaper and faster.

Public cloud also makes it easier to launch globally without building global data centers.

It supports rapid growth,which is why startups love it,but it also supports rapid modernization,which is why enterprises use it too.

In many ways,public cloud turned infrastructure into something you can request on demand.

This shift made IT more agile and more scalable.

Public cloud reduces upfront cost because you don't buy infrastructure first,and that can be a massive business advantage.

You pay for what you use,which can reduce wasted capacity,especially for workloads that change a lot.

However,you have to manage your usage because small costs can add up if resources run 24 by 7.

Cloud cost management becomes its own skill,tracking usage,shutting down unused resources and choosing the right size for workloads.

Public cloud often turns capital expense into operating expense,which many organizations prefer.

The win is flexibility,but the risk is surprise bills if governance is weak.

Public cloud is commonly used for web hosting,application backends,dev and test environments,backups and disaster recovery.

It's also used for data processing,analytics and modern app architectures where you want scalable services instead of managing servers.

Another big use case is burst workloads,times when you need extra capacity temporarily,like sales events or seasonal demand.

Public cloud is a good fit when workload demand is unpredictable or when speed matters.

It's also useful when you want access to managed services like hosted databases and messaging systems.In short,public cloud shines when you want speed,scale and service variety.

One of the strongest public cloud benefits is elasticity.

You can scale up when demand spikes and scale down when demand drops.

This can happen automatically if you design systems to do it,which helps with both performance and cost.In a traditional data center,scaling might mean buying servers and waiting weeks.

In public cloud,scaling is often a configuration choice and a few clicks.

This changes how you design applications because you can plan for growth without buying maximum capacity on day one.

It also helps reliability because you can spread workloads across multiple resources.

Elasticity is one of the reasons public cloud became the default for modern internet services.

Public cloud providers have data centers in many geographic regions,which makes it easier to serve customers close to where they live.

This improves performance because distance affects latency,especially for real-time applications.

Global infrastructure also supports resilience because you can build systems that survive failures by running in multiple locations.

Even if you only run in one region,you can often design with redundancy inside that region.

This is much harder for most companies to do alone.

Global reach is one of the most quietly powerful features of public cloud.

It helps both performance and business continuity.

Public cloud can be very secure,but it demands correct configuration.

The provider handles the security of the underlying infrastructure,but customers still control access to their resources.

Identity and access management becomes critical because many cloud incidents come from overly permissive accounts or exposed services.

Logging,monitoring,and strong authentication practices matter a lot because cloud environments change quickly.

Another key is data protection.

Encryption and backup should be planned,not assumed.

Public cloud security is a partnership between provider controls and customer choices.

If your access controls are sloppy,the cloud will not save you.

Public cloud is not just virtual machines,it's an ecosystem of managed services.

Managed databases,object storage,monitoring services,serverless functions,and AI tools are common building blocks.

These services reduce the need to run everything yourself and they can speed up development.

The trade-off is that you learn provider-specific services which can create some dependency.

Many organizations accept this because the productivity gains are real.

Public cloud is often about using managed services wisely,not rebuilding everything from scratch.

The more you rely on managed services,the less time you spend on routine infrastructure work.

Public cloud has downsides that you should know upfront.

Cost surprises can happen if resources are left running or data transfer patterns aren't understood.

Vendor lock-in can happen if you build heavily around one provider's specialized services.

Governance can be difficult if teams create resources without standards or documentation.

Network dependency matters too.

If your connectivity is poor,your user experience will suffer.

And like any environment,misconfiguration can create security issues.

The good news is that these challenges are manageable with good planning.

Public cloud works best when you treat it as an engineered environment,not a magical utility.

Public cloud is great for small organizations because it avoids large upfront purchases and allows quick growth.

It's also great for large organizations because it supports global deployments,rapid experimentation and modernization projects.

The difference is scale of governance.

Bigger organizations need stronger policies,stronger access control design and better cost tracking.

Small organizations can move fast,but they still need basic discipline so costs and security don't spiral.

Either way,public cloud offers flexibility that traditional data centers struggle to match.

The key is aligning cloud usage with real business needs and real operational maturity.

Public cloud is powerful,but it rewards good planning.

Great job.

Public cloud is shared infrastructure provided by companies like AWS,Azure and Google Cloud,built for speed,global reach,and pay-as-you-go flexibility.

It lets you provision resources quickly,scale up and down,and access a huge ecosystem of managed services.

The main responsibilities you keep are configuration,access control,and managing your usage so costs stay predictable.

The main risks are cost surprises,misconfiguration and governance problems if teams aren't coordinated.

Now that you have seen private cloud and public cloud,the next step is combining them.

Next up we'll talk about hybrid cloud where organizations mix private and public environments to get the best fit for each workload.

190. 混合云

大家好，今天我们要讨论的是混合云，顾名思义，就是将私有云和公有云混合在一起。

许多组织不会全盘采用单一模型，因为不同的系统有不同的需求。

混合云让你能够将某些工作负载保留在私有环境中，同时将其他工作负载使用公有云。

其目标是将每个工作负载放置在最符合安全、成本和性能要求的地方。

这在真实的企业中极为常见，因为它们已经拥有数据中心，但同时也希望获得云的灵活性。

混合云基本上是一种面向现实的策略，而不是追求完美的策略。

混合云意味着你至少拥有两个环境：私有环境和公有环境，并且它们以支持实际工作流程的方式连接在一起。

这种连接可能是网络连接、身份集成、共享监控或数据同步。

仅仅因为你有一些系统在本地而另一些系统在云端，这并不叫混合云。

混合云意味着经过深思熟虑的设计，以便它们能够协同工作。

有些组织将数据库保留在私有环境中，而在公有云中运行Web前端。

另一些组织则将核心业务系统保留在私有环境中，并使用公有云进行备份和灾难恢复。

重要的是，混合云是经过规划的，而非偶然形成的。

如果是偶然形成的，它就会变得混乱且难以保障安全。

采用混合云的最大原因是，并非所有系统都能以相同的速度迁移。

有些系统有合规性要求、数据驻留规则或遗留架构，这使得迁移变得困难。

而其他系统则能从公有云的扩展能力和托管服务中获益巨大。

混合云让你能够逐步现代化，而不是进行高风险的“大爆炸”式迁移。

它还允许你在保持对敏感数据更严格控制的同时，利用公有云进行创新。

混合云往往是连接我们当前状态与理想状态的桥梁。

它是一种既能降低风险又能推动进步的策略。

当你明确决定什么内容该放在哪里时，混合云的效果最好。

敏感数据库、受监管的工作负载以及对延迟或控制有严格要求的系统通常保留在私有环境中。

面向客户的应用程序、可扩展的Web服务和分析工作负载通常会迁移到公有云。

有些工作负载会被拆分，例如通过安全连接将数据保留在私有端，而在云端进行处理。

关键在于设计时要设定明确的边界和清晰的所有权。

如果团队就放置规则无法达成一致，混合云就会变得混乱不堪。

优秀的混合云设计与其说是关于技术，不如说是关于明智的工作负载决策。

混合云的一个巨大挑战是数据移动。

如果你的应用程序在公有云中，而数据库在本地，那么每个请求都可能需要跨越环境。

这可能会产生延迟、成本以及可靠性依赖问题。

数据同步也很棘手。

如果两个环境需要相同的数据，你必须确定哪一个是事实来源。

有些组织使用缓存或复制来减少跨环境的通信。

另一些组织则重新设计应用程序，使数据更靠近计算资源。

在混合云中，数据架构与基础设施同等重要。

许多混合云问题实际上是数据放置问题。混合云需要环境之间的安全连接。

许多组织使用加密的虚拟专用网络隧道，而大型组织通常使用专用连接以获得更好的可靠性和性能。

必须规划路由、域名系统解析和防火墙规则，以便系统能够安全通信。

连接还需要冗余，因为如果链路故障，你的混合工作流程可能会停止。

监控连接变得与监控服务器同样重要。

这就是为什么网络团队在混合云成功中扮演着巨大角色。

混合云既是一个网络项目，也是一个云项目。

混合云通常需要在私有和公有系统之间保持一致的身份和访问控制。如果用户在每个环境中都有单独的账户，安全就会变得混乱，入职流程也会变得痛苦。

许多组织旨在实现单点登录，以便身份集中管理、访问可审计且权限一致。

这也有助于在有人离开组织时撤销访问权限。

身份集成减少了困惑并降低了风险。

在混合环境中，身份是保持访问可控的粘合剂。

如果身份是碎片化的，混合云就变得更难控制。

混合云增加了复杂性，因为你正在运营两个不同的环境，通常使用不同的工具和仪表板。

你需要一致的监控，以便能够检测两侧的停机、减速和安全问题。

日志记录应该集中化，以便调查事件时无需在平台之间跳转。补丁策略和配置标准需要保持一致，否则你会出现漂移，导致两侧随时间推移变得不同。

混合云也会影响故障排除，因为问题可能出现在公有云、私有云或它们之间的连接中。

这就是为什么混合云需要强大的运营纪律。

它可能很强大，但绝非“设置好就忘”。

混合环境的安全性取决于其最薄弱的一侧。

如果私有侧防护严密，但公有侧访问权限过宽，攻击者就会针对公有侧下手。

混合云安全需要在加密、分段、日志记录和特权访问方面制定一致的策略。

你还需要明确的数据移动和数据分类规则。

另一个关键是共同责任意识。

公有云仍然需要客户仔细配置。

混合云通常会增加攻击面，因为有更多的组件和更多的连接。

好消息是，良好的策略设计可以控制这种风险。

混合云安全关乎一致性，而不仅仅是工具。

混合云常用于灾难恢复，即私有系统将备份复制到公有云以实现弹性。

它也用于渐进式迁移，即应用程序的部分内容随时间逐步迁移，而不是一次性全部迁移。

另一个用例是云爆发，即工作负载在需求高峰期间扩展到公有云，随后再缩减。

当组织希望将敏感数据保留在私有环境中，同时在公有云中运行分析或Web服务时，也会使用混合云。

许多企业在私有环境中运行内部身份系统，同时使用公有云服务来处理应用程序和协作。

模式始终如一。

保留必须受控的内容，扩展可以共享的内容。

混合云是适合许多真实企业的务实妥协方案。

混合云可能很困难，因为集成工作是实实在在的工程设计工作。

网络设计、身份集成、数据同步和一致监控都需要时间和规划。

技能要求可能更广泛，因为团队必须既了解私有基础设施，又了解公有云服务。

故障排除更加困难，因为故障可能发生在环境之间的边界上。

变更控制也变得棘手，因为一侧的更新可能会破坏与另一侧的集成。

这就是为什么混合云项目在拥有清晰的架构和明确的所有权时最容易成功。

混合云很强大，但它并非免费的。

如果没有良好的治理，混合云可能会变得昂贵或混乱。

团队需要命名标准、标签、访问控制以及关于谁可以创建什么的明确规则。

成本跟踪很重要，因为公有云支出可能会悄然增长，而私有云成本则是固定且持续的。

良好的治理还包括文档、标准化模板以及定期审查正在运行的内容及其原因。

如果没有治理，混合云就会变成两个云加上混乱。

有了治理，混合云就成为一种灵活、安全的策略。

如果你保持环境对齐并加以管理，混合云将成为长期的优势。

做得好。

混合云是关于结合私有和公有环境，以便工作负载可以生活在最适合它们的地方。它之所以流行，是因为它支持渐进式迁移，将敏感系统置于更强的控制之下，并在需要时提供公有云的可扩展性。

其最大的优势是灵活性和务实的现代化，而最大的挑战是集成复杂性、连接依赖性以及一致的安全管理。

当你将网络、身份、数据放置、监控和治理作为一个整体设计来规划时，混合云的效果最好。

既然你已经了解了私有云、公有云和混合云，还有一个部署模型需要了解。

接下来，我们将介绍社区云，即特定的一组组织为共同目标共享云基础设施。

英文原文

Hey everyone,today we are talking hybrid cloud,which is exactly what it sounds like,mixing private cloud and public cloud together.

Many organizations don't go all in on one model because different systems have different needs.

Hybrid cloud lets you keep certain workloads private while using public cloud for others.

The goal is to place each workload where it makes the most sense for security,cost and performance.

This is extremely common in real enterprises because they already have data centers but also want cloud flexibility.

Hybrid cloud is basically a strategy for reality,not a strategy for perfection.

Hybrid cloud means you have at least two environments,private and public,and they are connected in a way that supports real workflows.

That connection might be networking,identity integration,shared monitoring or data synchronization.

It's not hybrid just because you have a few systems on-prem and a few systems in cloud.

Hybrid implies deliberate design so they can work together.

Some organizations keep databases private while running web front ends in public cloud.

Others keep core business systems private and use public cloud for backups and disaster recovery.

The important part is that hybrid is planned,not accidental.

If it's accidental,it becomes messy and hard to secure.

The biggest reason for hybrid cloud is that not everything can move at the same speed.

Some systems have compliance requirements,data residency rules or legacy architectures that make migration hard.

Other systems benefit massively from public cloud scaling and managed services.

Hybrid lets you modernize gradually instead of doing a risky big bang migration.

It also allows you to keep sensitive data under tighter control while still using public cloud for innovation.

Hybrid is often the bridge between where we are and where we want to be.

It's a strategy that reduces risk while enabling progress.

Hybrid cloud works best when you clearly decide what belongs where.

Sensitive databases,regulated workloads and systems with strict latency or control requirements often stay private.

Customer-facing apps,scalable web services and analytics workloads often move to public cloud.

Some workloads are split like keeping data private while processing in the cloud with secure connections.

The key is designing with intentional boundaries and clear ownership.

If teams don't agree on placement rules,hybrid becomes chaotic.

Good hybrid design is less about technology and more about smart workload decisions.

A big challenge in hybrid is data movement.

If your application is in public cloud but your database is on-prem,every request may have to cross environments.

That can create latency,costs and reliability dependencies.

Data synchronization is also tricky.

If two environments need the same data,you must decide which one is the source of truth.

Some organizations use caching or replication to reduce cross-environment chatter.

Others redesign apps to keep data closer to compute.

In hybrid cloud,data architecture matters as much as infrastructure.

Many hybrid problems are actually data placement problems.Hybrid cloud requires secure connectivity between environments.

Many organizations use encrypted VPN tunnels,and larger organizations often use dedicated connections for better reliability and performance.

Routing,DNS,and firewall rules must be planned so systems can communicate safely.

Connectivity also needs redundancy because if your link fails,your hybrid workflows may stop.

Monitoring the connection becomes as important as monitoring servers.

This is why network teams play a huge role in hybrid success.

Hybrid cloud is often a networking project as much as it is a cloud project.

Hybrid cloud usually needs consistent identity and access control across private and public systems.If users have separate accounts in each environment,security becomes messy and onboarding becomes painful.

Many organizations aim for single sign-on so identity is centralized,access is audited and permissions are consistent.

This also helps with removing access when someone leaves the organization.

Identity integration reduces confusion and reduces risk.

In hybrid environments,identity is the glue that keeps access manageable.

If identity is fragmented,hybrid becomes harder to control.

Hybrid adds complexity because you are operating two different environments,often with different tools and dashboards.

You need consistent monitoring so you can detect outages,slowdowns and security issues across both sides.

Logging should be centralized so incidents can be investigated without jumping between platforms.Patch policies and configuration standards need to be consistent or you will get drift where each side becomes different over time.

Hybrid also affects troubleshooting because a problem might be in public cloud,private cloud or the connection between them.

This is why hybrid requires strong operational discipline.

It can be powerful but it's not set it and forget it.

A hybrid environment is only as secure as its weakest side.

If the private side is locked down but the public side has overly permissive access,attackers will go after the public side.

Hybrid security requires consistent policies for encryption,segmentation,logging and privileged access.

You also need clear rules for data movement and data classification.

Another key is shared responsibility awareness.

Public cloud still requires careful customer configuration.

Hybrid often increases the attack surface because there are more components and more connections.

The good news is that good policy design can control that risk.

Hybrid security is about consistency,not just tools.

Hybrid cloud is common for disaster recovery where private systems replicate backups into public cloud for resilience.

It's also used for gradual migrations where parts of an application move over time instead of all at once.

Another use case is cloud bursting where workloads expand into public cloud during peak demand and shrink afterward.

Hybrid is also used when organizations want to keep sensitive data private but run analytics or web services in public cloud.

Many enterprises run internal identity systems privately while using public cloud services for apps and collaboration.

The pattern is always the same.

Keep what must be controlled and scale what can be shared.

Hybrid cloud is the practical compromise that fits many real businesses.

Hybrid can be difficult because integration work is real engineering work.

Network design,identity integration,data synchronization and consistent monitoring take time and planning.

Skill requirements can be broader because teams must know both private infrastructure and public cloud services.

Troubleshooting is harder because failures can happen at the boundary between environments.

Change control also becomes tricky because updates on one side may break integration with the other side.

This is why hybrid projects succeed best when they have clear architecture and clear ownership.

Hybrid cloud is powerful but it's not free.

Hybrid cloud can become expensive or messy without good governance.

Teams need naming standards,tagging,access controls and clear rules for who can create what.

Cost tracking is important because public cloud spend can grow quietly while private cloud costs are fixed and ongoing.

Good governance also includes documentation,standardized templates and regular reviews of what is running and why.

Without governance,hybrid becomes two clouds plus confusion.

With governance,hybrid becomes a flexible,secure strategy.

If you keep environments aligned and managed,hybrid cloud becomes a long-term advantage.

Great work.

Hybrid cloud is about combining private and public environments so workloads can live where they fit best.It's popular because it supports gradual migration,keeps sensitive systems under stronger control,and still provides public cloud scalability when needed.

The biggest strengths are flexibility and realistic modernization,while the biggest challenges are integration complexity,connectivity dependency,and consistent security management.

Hybrid works best when you plan networking,identity,data placement,monitoring,and governance as a single design.

Now that you understand private,public and hybrid,there's one more deployment model to know.

Next up we'll cover Community Cloud where a specific group of organizations shares cloud infrastructure for common goals.

191. 社区云

大家好！

社区云就像是为具有相似需求的一组特定组织构建的共享云环境。

它不像公有云那样任何人都可以加入，也不像私有云那样仅由一个组织拥有，社区云是在一个定义明确的社区内共享的。

这个社区可能是医院、大学、研究实验室或政府组织，它们需要类似的安全性和合规性规则。

其理念是在保持比一般公有云更强控制力的同时，共享成本和共享标准。

它不是最常见的模型，但很重要，因为它出现在受监管和协作的环境中。

如果你理解了其中的原因，社区云就完全说得通了。

社区云的存在是因为私有云对一个组织来说可能太昂贵，而公有云对于特殊需求来说可能感觉太开放或太通用。

当多个组织共享类似的法规时，共同构建某些东西可能更高效。

他们可以就安全基线、审计实践和符合其行业的治理规则达成一致。

通过共享环境，他们可以减少重复工作，同时保持比随机公有云客户更强的一致性。

这基本上就是“让我们联手吧，因为我们都需要同样的东西”。

当合规要求严格且标准化控制有益时，这一点尤其具有吸引力。

社区云是共享的，但它不是谁都可以随意使用的。

成员资格仅限于符合社区规则、合同和安全期望的组织。

参与组织通常会就如何管理身份、如何分类数据以及如何审计访问权限达成一致。

因为参与者是已知的实体，所以治理可以比在一般公共环境中更强。

话虽如此，共享仍然需要明确的边界，因此一个成员无法访问另一个成员的数据。

社区云依赖于技术隔离和组织信任。它是带有商定规则的共享基础设施，而不是随意的共享。

社区云通常出现在每个人都有类似合规需求的行业中。

医疗组织可能希望拥有遵循共同隐私和安全要求的共享系统。

大学和研究机构可能希望为实验室和科学工作负载共享计算资源。

政府社区有时会构建围绕严格控制and审计设计的专用环境。

因为需求相似，所以可以针对该社区调整环境，而不是试图服务于所有人。

这可以减少摩擦并加速常见解决方案的部署。

在许多情况下，价值不仅仅在于基础设施。

而在于共享标准和共享治理。

当协作是一个目标而不仅仅是节省成本时，社区云尤其有价值。

如果多个组织正在从事联合研究、共享数据项目或跨机构服务，拥有一个共享环境可以减少集成的麻烦。

与其在独立的云之间构建复杂的桥梁，不如让社区在一个受治理的环境中运营。

协作仍然需要仔细的权限和数据控制，但基础设施的设计初衷就是考虑到共享使用。

这可以加速那些否则会在安全和集成延迟中陷入停滞的项目。

简而言之，当协作是任务的一部分时，社区云会有所帮助。

社区云最困难的部分不是服务器，而是治理。

社区必须就谁支付什么费用、谁制定策略、如何批准变更以及如何处理争端达成一致。

信任至关重要，因为如果治理马虎，一个薄弱的成员可能会给整个环境带来风险。

强有力的规则、审计和明确的责任制变得必不可少。

这就是为什么社区云不如公有云常见。

它需要合作和正式协议。

但当组织保持一致时，它可以运作得非常好。

社区云是一个需要强大组织团队协作的技术解决方案。

社区云在成本和控制方面通常介于公有云和私有云之间。

它的成本可能高于公有云，因为它无法受益于同样的大规模效应，但它可能比私有云便宜，因为成本由多个成员分担。

在控制方面，它通常提供比公有云更一致的治理，因为社区可以设定符合其需求的标准。

然而，这也意味着妥协。

成员可能无法完全按照自己的意愿行事。

社区必须在灵活性和标准化之间取得平衡。

这种平衡正是社区云得以运作的关键。

社区云中的安全有两个层面：技术隔离和社区策略执行。

环境必须隔离每个组织的数据和工作负载，以免共享成为安全问题。

同时，社区必须在所有成员中强制执行强大的身份管理和访问控制。

监控和审计尤为重要，因为涉及多个组织。

如果事件响应流程不明确，问题会迅速恶化。社区云可以非常安全，但这取决于一致的标准和严格的治理。

当设计良好时，它成为受监管协作的强大解决方案。

当成员在优先级、预算或变更时间表上存在分歧时，社区云可能会陷入困境。

一个组织可能希望快速更新功能，而另一个组织则希望严格稳定并缓慢变更。

定义共同责任也可能很困难，即在停机或安全事件期间谁负责什么以及谁承担责任。

另一个挑战是扩展。

增长需要协调和影响多个组织的投资决策。

如果社区不一致，这种模式可能会令人沮丧。

这就是为什么社区云从第一天起就需要强大的治理结构。

如果没有这一点，共享环境就会变成共同的头痛问题。

识别社区云的一个快速方法是问：多个组织是否共享相同的合规要求，并希望为了共同的目标共享基础设施？

如果是，社区云可能适合。

另一个线索是组织间反复出现的重复工作，即每个人都在单独构建类似的系统。

如果共享平台可以在满足严格规则的同时减少重复，社区云就会变得具有吸引力。

当协作内置于任务中时也很常见，例如研究网络或多机构服务。

目标是安全高效地共享，而不是随意共享。

社区云是针对特殊情况的专业模型。

社区云是关于多个组织共享一个环境，而混合云是关于一个组织混合其私有和公共环境。

人们有时会混淆这两者，但“谁拥有它”这个问题可以澄清这一点。

在社区云中，所有权和治理由具有共同需求的一组组织共享。

在混合云中，治理通常在一个组织内部，挑战在于私有和公共之间的集成。

两种模型都涉及协调和策略，但协调方式不同。

社区云关乎多组织治理。

混合云关乎多环境集成。

了解这种差异可以防止在考试和实际项目中产生许多困惑。

当你有一个定义明确的组织群体，它们彼此之间有足够信任来进行合作并共享治理时，社区云就有意义了。

当合规需求相似且可以标准化时，它也适用。

当需要协作且共享基础设施将简化集成时，它变得特别有价值。

但对于只想快速获取云服务的随机企业来说，它通常不是首选。

社区云是为具有共同目标的特定社区量身定制的模型。

当这些条件存在时，它可以成为一个很好的解决方案。

当这些条件不存在时，公有云或私有云可能更容易。

太棒了。

社区云是为具有共同需求的一组特定组织构建的共享云基础设施。

它介于公有云和私有云之间，比公有云更专业且受治理，但与私有云不同，它是共享和协作的。

最大的好处是共享成本、共享标准和更轻松的协作，而最大的挑战是多个组织之间的治理、信任和协调。

如果社区能在规则和责任制上达成一致，社区云既可以安全又高效。

既然我们已经完成了主要部署模型的学习，现在准备深入探讨具体的云服务。

接下来，我们将深入探讨基础设施即服务，并讨论云中的虚拟机、存储和网络。

英文原文

Hey everyone!

Community cloud is like a shared cloud environment built for a specific group of organizations that have similar needs.

Instead of anyone can join like public cloud and instead of only one organization owns it like private cloud,community cloud is shared among a defined community.

The community might be hospitals,universities,research labs or government organizations that need similar security and compliance rules.

The idea is to share costs and share standards while still keeping things more controlled than a general public cloud.

It's not the most common model,but it's important because it shows up in regulated and collaborative environments.

If you understand the why,community cloud makes perfect sense.

Community cloud exists because private cloud can be too expensive for one organization,while public cloud can feel too open or too generic for specialized requirements.

When multiple organizations share similar regulations,it can be more efficient to build something together.

They can agree on security baselines,audit practices,and governance rules that fit their industry.

By sharing the environment,they can reduce duplicated effort while maintaining stronger alignment than random public cloud customers.

It's basically let's team up because we all need the same thing.

This is especially appealing when compliance requirements are strict and standardized controls are beneficial.

A community cloud is shared,but it's not a free-for-all.

Membership is limited to organizations that meet the community's rules,contracts,and security expectations.

The participating organizations often agree on how identity is managed,how data is classified,and how access is audited.

Because the participants are known entities,governance can be stronger than in a general public environment.

That said,sharing still requires clear boundaries,so one member cannot access another member's data.

Community cloud depends on both technical isolation and organizational trust.It's shared infrastructure with agreed rules,not random sharing.

Community cloud often appears in industries where everyone has similar compliance needs.

Healthcare organizations may want shared systems that follow common privacy and security requirements.

Universities and research institutions may want shared compute resources for labs and scientific workloads.

Government communities sometimes build dedicated environments designed around strict controls and auditing.

Because the needs are similar,the environment can be tuned for that community instead of trying to serve everyone.

This can reduce friction and speed up deployment of common solutions.

In many cases,the value is not just the infrastructure.

It's the shared standards and shared governance.

Community cloud is especially valuable when collaboration is a goal,not just cost savings.

If multiple organizations are working on joint research,shared data projects,or cross-agency services,having a shared environment can reduce integration headaches.

Instead of building complex bridges between separate clouds,the community can operate within one governed environment.

Collaboration still requires careful permissions and data controls,but the infrastructure is designed with shared use in mind.

This can speed up projects that would otherwise get stuck in security and integration delays.

In short,community cloud helps when working together is part of the mission.

The hardest part of community cloud is not the servers,it's governance.

The community must agree on who pays for what,who sets policies,how changes are approved,and how disputes are handled.

Trust matters because a weak member could create risk for the whole environment if governance is sloppy.

Strong rules,audits,and clear accountability become essential.

This is why community cloud is less common than public cloud.

It takes cooperation and formal agreements.

But when the organizations are aligned,it can work extremely well.

Community cloud is a technical solution that requires strong organizational teamwork.

Community cloud usually lands between public and private in both cost and control.

It may cost more than public cloud because it does not benefit from the same massive scale,but it can be cheaper than private cloud because costs are shared among multiple members.

In terms of control,it often offers more aligned governance than public cloud because the community can set standards that match its needs.

However,it also means compromise.

Members may not get everything exactly their way.

The community must balance flexibility with standardization.

That balance is what makes community cloud work.

Security in a community cloud has two layers:technical isolation and community policy enforcement.

The environment must isolate each organization's data and workloads so the sharing doesn't become a security problem.

At the same time,the community must enforce strong identity management and access controls across all members.

Monitoring and auditing are especially important because multiple organizations are involved.

If incident response processes are unclear,problems get worse fast.Community cloud can be very secure,but it depends on consistent standards and strict governance.

When designed well,it becomes a strong solution for regulated collaboration.

Community cloud can struggle when members disagree on priorities,budgets,or change timelines.

One organization may want rapid feature updates while another wants strict stability and slow changes.

It can also be hard to define shared responsibility,who handles what and who is accountable during outages or security events.

Another challenge is scaling.

Growth requires coordination and investment decisions that affect multiple organizations.

If the community is not aligned,the model can become frustrating.

This is why Community Cloud requires a strong governance structure from day one.

Without that,the shared environment becomes a shared headache.

A quick way to recognize Community Cloud is to ask:do multiple organizations share the same compliance requirements and want shared infrastructure for a shared purpose?

If yes,Community Cloud might fit.

Another clue is repeated duplicated effort across organizations where everyone is building similar systems separately.

If a shared platform would reduce duplication while still meeting strict rules,community cloud becomes attractive.

It is also common when collaboration is built into the mission,like research networks or multi-agency services.

The goal is to share safely and efficiently,not to share randomly.

Community cloud is a specialized model for specialized situations.

Community cloud is about multiple organizations sharing one environment,while hybrid cloud is about one organization mixing its private and public environments.

People sometimes confuse these,but the who owns it question clears it up.

In community cloud,ownership and governance are shared among a group with common needs.

In hybrid cloud,governance is typically inside one organization,and the challenge is integration between private and public.

Both models involve coordination and policy,but the coordination is different.

Community is about multi-organization governance.

Hybrid is about multi-environment integration.

Knowing the difference prevents a lot of confusion on exams and in real projects.

Community cloud makes sense when you have a defined group of organizations that trust each other enough to cooperate and share governance.

It also fits when compliance needs are similar and can be standardized.

It becomes especially valuable when collaboration is required and shared infrastructure will simplify integration.

But it's usually not the first choice for a random business that just wants cloud services quickly.

Community cloud is a purpose-built model for a specific community with shared goals.

When those conditions exist,it can be a great solution.

When they don't,public cloud or private cloud may be easier.

Awesome.

Community cloud is shared cloud infrastructure built for a specific group of organizations with common requirements.

It sits between public and private,more specialized and governed than public,but shared and cooperative unlike private.

The biggest benefits are shared cost,shared standards,and easier collaboration,while the biggest challenges are governance,trust,and coordination across multiple organizations.

If the community can agree on rules and accountability,Community Cloud can be both secure and efficient.

Now that we have finished the main deployment models,we are ready to go deeper into specific cloud services.

Next up,we'll dive into infrastructure as a service and talk about virtual machines,storage and networking in the cloud.

192. 基础设施即服务（IaaS）

大家好，是时候深入探讨基础设施即服务了，它基本上就是在云中租用虚拟计算机，而不是购买物理服务器。

你仍然获得了真实的计算能力、真实的存储和真实的网络。

只不过这些是通过提供商的数据中心交付的。

最大的区别在于速度。

你无需等待数天或数周来获取硬件，只需几分钟即可创建一台服务器。

这就是为什么基础设施即服务成为许多云之旅的起点。

在本讲座中，我们将保持务实，谈谈你得到了什么、你需要管理什么以及它为何有用。

使用基础设施即服务，你会获得三个主要构建模块：虚拟机、存储和网络。

虚拟机就是你的服务器，你通过选择中央处理器、内存和磁盘大小来决定它的性能有多强。

存储是你数据存放的地方，根据你的具体操作，通常有多种存储类型可供选择。

网络是你的服务器连接的方式，包括子网、防火墙规则，有时还包括将流量分散到多台服务器上的负载均衡器。

提供商为你提供快速创建这些资源的平台，但你仍然要对自己安装的内容、如何保护它以及如何维护它负责。

基础设施即服务中的虚拟机表现就像一台普通的服务器。

它有操作系统，有文件系统，运行应用程序，并且像任何其他服务器一样，可以被更新或配置错误。

你可以运行Windows或Linux，并安装你的工作负载所需的任何软件。

你还可以调整虚拟机的大小，这意味着你可以在不购买新硬件的情况下增加中央处理器或内存。

当服务器性能不足且运行缓慢时，这非常有用。

但请记住，因为它仍然是你的服务器，所以修补它、保护它和监控它的仍然是你。

基础设施即服务给了你灵活性，但它并没有消除管理工作。

一个常见的基础设施即服务例子是亚马逊云科技的弹性计算云，你可以在其中选择符合你需求的实例类型。

你可能会为轻量级工作负载选择小型虚拟机，或者为大型数据库或处理作业等重型工作负载选择大得多的虚拟机。

你还要选择操作系统，启动它，虚拟机很快就会可用，通常大约在一分钟内。

在你的例子中，你提到了一个小型实例，比如两个中央处理器、两吉字节内存，以及一个大型实例，比如九十六个中央处理器和三百八十四吉字节内存，这是展示范围有多广的绝佳方式。

主要理念很简单。

你租用的服务器可以很小也可以很大，并且你可以根据需求的变化改变大小。

通过选择更大的服务器来实现这种扩展，是基础设施即服务最实用的优势之一。

Azure虚拟机和谷歌计算引擎遵循相同的核心概念。

选择大小，选择操作系统，启动虚拟机，然后像管理服务器一样管理它。

名称和仪表板可能不同，但在所有提供商中，其理念是相同的。

你通常会发现，在已经使用微软系统的组织中，Azure非常舒适，并且它通常能与企业身份系统和Windows工作负载顺畅集成。

谷歌云遵循相同的模式，并提供类似的基于虚拟机的基础设施服务。

在现实生活中，一旦你理解了基础设施即服务模型，你就能更快地学习不同的提供商。

它变成了相同的理念，只是菜单不同。

基础设施即服务为你提供多种存储选择，选择正确的存储至关重要。

块存储就像附加到虚拟机的虚拟硬盘，通常用于需要传统磁盘的操作系统和应用程序数据。

对象存储更适合存储大量文件，如图像、备份、日志和媒体，并且它的扩展性极佳。

文件存储的作用就像多个服务器可以访问的共享网络驱动器，当多台机器需要相同文件时非常有用。

大多数云设计会使用不止一种存储类型，因为每种类型解决不同的问题。

最简单的记忆方法是：块存储是附加磁盘，对象存储是大型存储桶，文件存储是共享文件夹。

基础设施即服务中的网络是许多现实世界错误发生的地方，因为它看起来很简单，直到变得不简单为止。

你创建虚拟网络，将服务器放入子网，并使用类似防火墙的规则控制入站和出站流量。

你可能还会使用负载均衡器，以便网站可以在多个虚拟机上运行，而不是依赖单个虚拟机。

当网络设计良好时，系统既安全又可靠。

当网络设计糟糕时，服务可能会意外暴露给互联网，或者系统在应该通信时无法通信。

因此，即使基础设施即服务是租用服务器，它也涉及设计安全的网络。

良好的网络决策是优秀云工作的重要组成部分。

在基础设施即服务中，你根据使用情况付费，这既是好处也是陷阱。

运行虚拟机通常按时间计费，而存储通常按你存储的数据量以及存储时长计费。

数据传输也可能产生费用，特别是当数据离开云环境时。

在你的例子中，你提到了一台虚拟机每小时约两美分，另一台每小时约四美元，这展示了成本如何随规模扩大。

小型虚拟机每月的费用可能在十到二十美元之间，而大型虚拟机的费用可能会攀升至数百甚至数千美元，具体取决于它们运行的时间长短。

最简单的省钱习惯是关闭你不需要的资源，不要让测试服务器永远运行。

当你需要完全控制操作系统和安装软件时，基础设施即服务是一个绝佳的选择。

对于将旧系统迁移到云端，它也非常棒，因为你可以保持相同的一般服务器设置，只是将其在租用的基础设施上运行。

它非常适合临时环境，如开发和测试，因为你可以快速启动它们，并在完成后删除它们。

当你想要构建自定义网络布局和安全控制时，基础设施即服务也很有用。

如果你是那种擅长管理服务器的团队，基础设施即服务会让你感觉熟悉。

它是经典的信息技术，只是交付得更快、更灵活。

一种非常常见的基础设施即服务迁移风格是“提升和转移”，这意味着移动现有应用程序而不重新设计它。

你无需重写应用程序使其成为云原生，而是将虚拟机或服务器工作负载移动到云端并在那里运行。

这种方法很受欢迎，因为它比重建一切更快。

缺点是它可能无法充分利用云原生功能，并且可能仍然携带旧设置存在的相同问题。

但作为第一步，它通常是务实且现实的。

许多组织先进行“提升和转移”，然后在工作负载稳定后再进行现代化改造。

在基础设施即服务中，提供商管理物理世界：数据中心建筑、电力、冷却、物理服务器和核心基础设施。

你管理虚拟服务器环境、操作系统更新、安全补丁、已安装的应用程序、虚拟机上的用户访问以及数据备份方式。

这就是云责任变得真实的地方，因为忘记修补虚拟机仍然是一个安全风险。

基础设施即服务给了你自由，但自由也意味着你也可能犯错。

一个优秀的基础设施即服务团队会有修补、监控和备份的例行程序。

如果你认为基础设施即服务是由别人处理的，你最终会吃亏。

几个习惯可以让基础设施即服务更安全、更轻松。

使用强大的访问控制，不要仅仅因为方便就赋予每个人管理员权限。

定期修补操作系统并保持时间表，以免它成为被遗忘的任务。

备份应该经过规划和测试，而不是想当然，因为拥有无法恢复的备份等同于没有备份。

监控性能和可用性，以便在用户抱怨之前及早发现问题。

最后，清理资源。

未使用的虚拟机和存储会随着时间的推移浪费资金。

当你将灵活性与纪律相结合时，基础设施即服务的效果最好。

做得太棒了。

今天你学习了基础设施即服务，即云计算中租用虚拟基础设施的一面。

你获得了虚拟机、多种存储类型和虚拟网络，并且可以通过改变大小或添加资源来快速扩展。

提供商处理物理基础设施，但你仍然要管理自己的操作系统、补丁、应用程序和备份。

当你需要控制和灵活性时，基础设施即服务非常完美，特别是对于迁移和自定义设置，但它需要真正的运营责任。

现在我们准备好迎接相反的感觉了。

不再是管理服务器，而是直接使用软件。

接下来，我们将涵盖软件即服务，以及它为何成为大多数企业的日常云模型。

英文原文

Hey everyone,time to dive deeper into IaaS which is basically renting virtual computers in the cloud instead of buying physical servers.

You're still getting real computing power,real storage and real networking.

It's just delivered through a provider's data center.

The big difference is speed.

Instead of waiting days or weeks for hardware,you can create a server in minutes.

This is why iaaaz became the starting point for many cloud journeys.

In this lecture,we'll keep it practical and talk about what you get,what you manage and why it's useful.

With IAAS,you get three main building blocks,virtual machines,storage and networking.

The virtual machine is your server and you choose how powerful it is by selecting CPU,RAM and disk size.

Storage is where your data lives and you usually have multiple storage types depending on what you are doing.

Networking is how your servers connect,subnets,firewall rules and sometimes load balancers that spread traffic across multiple servers.

The provider gives you the platform to create these resources quickly,but you are still responsible for what you install,how you secure it and how you maintain it.

A virtual machine in IaaaS behaves like a normal server.

It has an operating system,it has a file system,it runs apps and it can be updated or misconfigured just like any other server.

You can run Windows or Linux and you can install whatever software your workload needs.

You can also resize VMs,meaning you can increase CPU or RAM without buying new hardware.

This is incredibly useful when a server is underpowered and performance is slow.

But remember,because it's still your server,you're still the one who patches it,secures it and monitors it.

IaaaS gives you flexibility,but it does not eliminate admin work.

A common IAS example is AWS EC2,where you pick an instance type that matches your needs.

You might choose a small VM for light workloads or a much larger VM for heavy workloads like large databases or processing jobs.

You also pick the operating system,launch it and the VM becomes available quickly,often in about a minute.

In your examples,you mentioned a small instance like 2 CPUs,2 GB RAM and a larger one like 96 CPUs and 384 GB RAM and that's a great way to show how wide the range can be.

The main idea is simple.

You are renting a server that can be tiny or massive and you can change sizes as your needs change.

That scale by choosing a bigger server is one of the most practical IAAS benefits.

Azure VMs and Google Compute Engine follow the same core concept.

Pick a size,pick an operating system,launch a VM and manage it like a server.

The names and dashboards differ but the idea is the same across providers.

you'll usually find that Azure is very comfortable in organizations that already use Microsoft systems,and it often integrates smoothly with enterprise identity and Windows workloads.

Google Cloud follows the same pattern and offers similar VM-based infrastructure services.

In real life,once you understand the IaaS model,you can learn different providers much faster.

It becomes the same idea,different menu.

IaaS gives you multiple storage choices,and choosing the right one matters.

Block storage is like a virtual hard drive attached to a VM,and it's commonly used for operating systems and application data that needs a traditional disk.

Object storage is better for storing lots of files like images,backups,logs,and media,and it scales extremely well.

File storage acts like a shared network drive that multiple servers can access,which is useful when multiple machines need the same files.

Most cloud designs use more than one storage type because each one solves a different problem.

The easiest way to remember it is:block is attached disk,object is big storage bucket,and file storage is shared folder.

Networking in IAS is where a lot of real-world mistakes happen because it looks simple until it isn't.

You create virtual networks,you place servers into subnets,and you control inbound and outbound traffic using firewall-like rules.

You might also use load balancers so a website can run across multiple VMs instead of relying on a single one.

When networking is done well,systems are both secure and reliable.

When networking is done poorly,services get exposed to the internet by accident,or systems can't communicate when they should.

So,even though IAS is renting servers,it's also designing safe networks.

Good networking decisions are a huge part of good cloud work.

In IaaS,you pay based on usage,and that's both the benefit and the trap.

Running VMs is commonly built by time,and storage is commonly built by how much you store and how long you store it.

Data transfer can also cost money,especially when data leaves the cloud environment.

In your example,you mentioned a VM around 2 cents per hour and another around$4 per hour,which shows how cost scales with size.

A small VM might land around$10 to$20 per month,while large VMs can climb into the hundreds or thousands depending on how long they run.

The simplest money-saving habit is turning off what you don't need and not leaving test servers running forever.

IAAS is a great choice when you need full control over the operating system and install software.

It's also great for moving older systems into the cloud because you can keep the same general server setup and just run it on rented infrastructure.

It works well for temporary environments like dev and test because you can spin them up quickly and delete them when finished.

IAAS is also useful when you want to build custom network layouts and security controls.

If you are the kind of team that's comfortable managing servers,IAAS feels familiar.

It's classic IT,just delivered faster and more flexibly.

A very common IAAS migration style is lift and shift,which means moving an existing application without redesigning it.

Instead of rewriting an app to be cloud native,you move the VM or the server workload to the cloud and run it there.

This approach is popular because it's quicker than rebuilding everything.

The downside is that it may not take full advantage of cloud native features and it can still carry the same problems the old setup had.

But as a first step,it's often practical and realistic.

Many organizations lift and shift first,then modernize later when the workload is stable.

In IaaS,the provider manages the physical world,the data center building,the power,the cooling,the physical servers,and the core infrastructure.

You manage the virtual server environment,operating system updates,security patches,installed applications,user access on the VM,and how data is backed up.

This is where cloud responsibility becomes real,because forgetting to patch a VM is still a security risk.

IaaaS gives you freedom,but freedom means you can also make mistakes.

A good IaaS team has routines for patching,monitoring,and backups.

If you treat IaaaS like someone else handles it,you'll eventually get burned.

A few habits make IaaaS safer and easier.

Use strong access controls and don't give everyone admin rights just because it's convenient.

Patch operating systems regularly and keep a schedule so it doesn't become a forgotten task.

Backups should be planned and tested,not assumed,because having a backup that can't restore is the same as not having a backup.

Monitor performance and availability so problems are detected early instead of after users complain.

And finally,clean up resources.

Unused VMs and storage waste money over time.

IaaaS works best when you combine flexibility with discipline.

Awesome work.

IAAS is perfect when you need control and flexibility especially for migrations and custom setups but it requires real operational responsibility.

193. 软件即服务（SaaS）

大家好，现在我们来谈谈软件即服务，这是最简单的云模型，因为你主要只是使用产品。

你无需构建服务器或部署代码，只需打开浏览器或应用程序，登录并开始工作。

这就是为什么软件即服务变得如此庞大。

它为客户移除了大部分技术设置工作。

人们时刻都在使用软件即服务，却往往没有意识到这一点。

正是这种模式让云成为日常商业工具的常态。

在本讲座中，我们将重点关注软件即服务能为你提供什么、你仍需管理什么以及需要注意什么。

使用软件即服务时，你无需构建基础设施，也无需维护平台。

你无需选择虚拟机大小，无需安装操作系统，也无需修补服务器。

更新由供应商处理，新功能可能会出现，而你无需安装任何东西。

从用户的角度来看，这很简单。

你访问工具并完成工作。

这对速度非常有利，因为你可以快速向团队推出软件。这也非常有利，因为小型组织可以使用企业级工具，而无需运行企业级基础设施。

软件即服务基本上就是作为服务交付的软件。

软件即服务通常采用订阅制，这意味着你按月或按年付费，通常是按用户付费。

这使得从小规模开始并在组织发展过程中随时间扩展变得更加容易。

在你的例子中，你提到了诸如办公类工具每位用户每月十二美元，以及Salesforce类工具每位用户每月七十五到三百美元这样的数字。

这些范围说明了价格如何因功能而异。

好处是没有巨大的前期购买成本，且采用速度更快。

坏处是，如果你不仔细管理许可，订阅费用多年累积起来可能很高。

软件即服务的预算编制变成了财务和用户管理的结合。

优秀的组织会像跟踪实物资产一样跟踪许可证。

即使供应商处理基础设施，你仍然需要管理重要的事情。

你需要管理用户账户、权限、角色访问，以及哪些人允许查看哪些数据。

你还需要管理设置、策略，有时还包括与其他系统的集成。数据治理很重要，因为你的数据存在于供应商的系统中，所以你需要制定关于共享、保留和访问的策略。

安全在实际层面上仍然是你的责任，特别是围绕密码、多因素身份验证和账户生命周期管理。

软件即服务减少了基础设施工作，但增加了身份和治理的重要性。

在软件即服务中，谁拥有访问权成为了最大的安全问题之一。

像Microsoft 365这样的生产力套件是软件即服务的绝佳例子，因为它取代了许多传统的本地软件和服务器。

组织可以使用基于云的电子邮件、协作和文件存储，而不是在内部运行邮件服务器和文件服务器。

你可以在笔记本电脑、手机或平板电脑上工作，你的文档可以随身携带。

协作是一个主要优势，因为多人可以在同一文件上工作，而无需来回发送电子邮件版本。

更新持续推出，因此功能会随着时间推移而改进，无需手动安装。

最大的成功因素是良好的用户和安全管理。

194. 平台即服务（PaaS）

大家好，今天我们来谈谈平台即服务，它旨在让你构建和运行应用程序，而无需管理底层基础设施。

在这种模式下，开发人员专注于编写代码和配置应用程序，而平台则处理许多与服务器相关的琐事。

就控制权和投入精力而言，平台即服务位于基础设施即服务和软件即服务之间。

你比软件即服务拥有更多的自由，因为你在构建自己的应用程序；但你的运营负担比基础设施即服务小，因为你无需管理每个服务器的细节。

平台即服务很受欢迎，因为它能帮助团队以更少的基础设施干扰更快地交付软件。

使用基础设施即服务时，你通常从构建服务器开始。

选择一台虚拟机，安装操作系统，配置运行时，设置Web服务器，打补丁，并进行维护。

这可能需要大量的设置工作，然后你才能部署应用程序的第一个版本。

使用平台即服务时，平台已经知道如何运行应用程序，因此你可以在基础设施设置上花费更少的时间。

这意味着更快的开发周期，以及更少的配置各不相同的独特服务器。

平台即服务就像跳过了建造厨房的步骤，转而使用一个已经设置好并维护好的厨房。

你仍然烹饪你的食谱，但你不必修理炉灶。

这就是为什么平台即服务对开发团队来说感觉像是一次生产力升级。Heroku是一个众所周知的例子，因为它让这个理念变得简单。

部署你的应用程序，它就能在线可用，而无需你手动构建服务器。

平台处理了大量的部署步骤，并提供了一个简单直接的工作流程。

重要的教训不是特定的命令或工具，而是无需自己构建基础设施的体验。

这就是为什么人们在快速移动时喜爱平台即服务的原因。它减少了让事物上线所需的管道工作量。

它还鼓励环境之间的一致性，从而使部署可重复。

对于想要速度的团队来说，这是一个主要优势。

Google App Engine是另一个例子，你部署应用程序，平台则在后台处理其运行方式。

根据服务的配置方式，平台可以在流量增长时扩展，并在流量下降时减少资源。

这有助于团队避免从头开始构建手动扩展系统。

最大的价值在于，开发人员可以更多地关注应用程序本身，而更少地关注管理服务器。

如果使用得当，这可以减少运营噪音并提高交付速度。

对于需求可能波动的Web应用程序和API来说，它特别有用。

平台即服务旨在吸收这些波动，而无需持续的行政工作。

平台即服务通常处理底层服务器、操作系统维护、运行时环境以及许多扩展和可用性功能。

这意味着与基础设施即服务相比，在操作系统层的补丁责任更少。

许多平台即服务还包括更轻松的日志记录、监控和部署流水线集成。

这减少了团队必须拼凑的单独工具的数量。

它还使标准化应用程序的部署、更新和监控变得更加容易。

平台成为应用程序运行的默认方式，从而提高了consistency。

简而言之，平台即服务从应用程序团队那里移除了大部分基础设施管理工作。

即使在平台即服务中，你仍然拥有应用程序逻辑、配置和数据决策的所有权。

你负责编写安全的代码、正确管理密钥，并控制谁有权访问应用程序。

你还负责处理应用程序更新、功能发布和测试实践。

在许多平台即服务环境中，你仍然必须决定你的应用程序如何使用存储、数据库和网络策略。

如果应用程序运行缓慢或有错误，那仍然是你的问题。

平台即服务减少了基础设施的琐事，但并不能消除对应用程序质量和数据保护的责任。

它只是将你的精力转移到更高层次的关注点上。

平台即服务非常适合Web应用程序、API和移动后端，其主要目标是快速交付功能。

当你的应用程序遵循现代模式并且可以在平台预期的环境中运行时，它的效果很好。

团队经常选择平台即服务，因为它使部署可重复且快速。它还有助于减少环境漂移，即一台服务器的配置与另一台不同。

对于许多企业来说，交付速度是一种竞争优势，而平台即服务直接支持这一点。

如果你需要频繁发布更新，平台即服务可能是一个强有力的匹配。

它是现代开发工作流程的实用工具。

平台即服务的主要权衡是你必须在平台的规则内工作。

你可能无法安装任何你想要的随机软件，或者以深层方式自定义操作系统。

如果你的应用程序需要非常复杂的设置，平台即服务可能无法干净地支持它。

这就是为什么一些团队在需要完全控制时仍然选择基础设施即服务。

但对于许多应用程序来说，平台的限制并不重要，速度带来的好处是值得的。

平台即服务是一种带有边界的便利选择模式。

如果你的应用程序适合该平台，这通常是一个巨大的胜利。

开发人员喜欢平台即服务的一个原因是，扩展和可靠性功能通常是内置的。

这不是魔法。

你仍然必须负责任地设计你的应用程序，但它移除了很多基础设施的复杂性。

平台即服务将运营繁重的工作转化为平台设置。

平台即服务的成本不仅仅关乎月度账单。

它还关乎工程时间。

如果平台即服务允许团队更快部署并花费更少时间修补服务器，那么即使服务定价看起来比原始虚拟机高，也可以降低总成本。平台即服务还可以减少由不一致的服务器维护引起的停机风险。

另一个优势是更简单的入职流程。

新团队成员无需学习基础设施的每个细节即可安全部署。

这加快了团队速度并提高了consistency。

权衡之处在于，你正在为平台的便利性和托管环境付费。

对于许多组织来说，这种交易是值得的。

当你需要构建自定义应用程序但不想承担管理服务器和操作系统的负担时，平台即服务是最佳选择。对于经常部署并希望获得可重复标准化部署的团队来说，它尤其出色。

当需要平滑且可预测的扩展而无需从头开始构建自定义自动化时，它也很有用。

如果你的应用程序符合标准Web应用程序模式，平台即服务通常能提供更快的结果。

如果你试图最小化运营干扰，平台即服务是一个强有力的工具。

它是现代应用程序开发非常常见的选择。

目标是快速交付，而无需手动构建每个基础设施层。

区分平台即服务和软件即服务的一个有用方法是问自己：你是在构建应用程序还是在使用应用程序？

使用软件即服务时，你使用的是成品，你的工作是管理用户和设置。

In this model,developers focus on writing code and configuring the app,while the platform handles many of the server-related chores.

PaaS sits between IaaS and SaaS in terms of control and effort.

You have more freedom than SaaS because you are building your own application,but you have less operational burden than IaaS because you are not managing every server detail.

PaaS is popular because it helps teams ship software faster with fewer infrastructure distractions.

With IaaS,you often start by building a server.

Pick a VM,install an OS,configure a runtime,set up a web server,patch it,and maintain it.

That can take a lot of setup before you even deploy your first version of the app.

With PaaS,the platform already knows how to run applications,so you spend less time on infrastructure setup.

That means faster development cycles and fewer snowflake servers that are all configured differently.

PaaS is like skipping the step of building the kitchen and instead using a kitchen that is already set up and maintained.

You still cook your recipe but you don't fix the stove.

That is why PaaS can feel like a productivity upgrade for development teams.Heroku is a well-known example because it made the idea feel easy.

Deploy your application and it becomes available online without you manually building servers.

The platform handles a lot of the deployment steps and provides a straightforward workflow.

The big lesson isn't the specific command or tool,it's the experience of not having to build the infrastructure yourself.

This is why people love PaaS when they are moving fast.It reduces the amount of plumbing work needed to get something live.

It also encourages consistency across environments so deployments are repeatable.

For teams that want speed,this is a major advantage.

Google App Engine is another example where you deploy your application and the platform handles how it runs behind the scenes.

The platform can scale when traffic grows and reduce resources when traffic drops depending on how the service is configured.

This helps teams avoid building manual scaling systems from scratch.

The big value is that developers can focus more on the app itself and less on managing servers.

When used correctly,this can reduce operational noise and increase delivery speed.

It's especially helpful for web apps and APIs where demand can fluctuate.

PaaS is built to absorb those fluctuations without constant admin work.

PaaS typically handles the underlying servers,operating system maintenance,runtime environments and many scaling and availability functions.

That means fewer patching responsibilities at the operating system layer compared to IaaS.

Many PaaS services also include easier integration with logging,monitoring and deployment pipelines.

This reduces the number of separate tools teams have to stitch together.

It also makes it easier to standardize how apps are deployed,updated,and monitored.

The platform becomes the default way apps run,which improves consistency.

In short,PaaS removes a big portion of infrastructure management from the application team.

Even in PaaS,you still own the application logic,the configuration,and the data decisions.

You are responsible for writing secure code,managing secrets correctly,and controlling who has access to the application.

You also handle application updates,feature releases,and testing practices.

In many PaaS environments,you must still decide how your application uses storage,databases,and networking policies.

If the application is slow or buggy,that's still your problem.

PaaS reduces infrastructure chores,but it does not eliminate responsibility for app quality and data protection.

It simply shifts your effort to higher level concerns.

PaaS is a great fit for web apps,APIs,and mobile backends,where the main goal is delivering features quickly.

It works well when your application follows modern patterns and can run inside the platform's expected environment.

Teams often choose PaaS because it makes deployments repeatable and fast.It also helps reduce environment drift where one server is configured differently than another.

For many businesses,speed of delivery is a competitive advantage,and PaaS directly supports that.

If you need to ship updates often,PaaS can be a strong match.

It's a practical tool for modern development workflows.

The main trade-off with PaaS is that you work within the platform's rules.

You may not be able to install any random software you want or customize the operating system in deep ways.

If your app needs a very complex setup,PaaS might not support it cleanly.

That's why some teams still choose IaaS when they need full control.

But for many applications,the platform limitations don't matter and the speed benefits are worth it.

PaaS is a choose convenience with boundaries model.

If your app fits the platform,it's usually a big win.

One reason developers like PaaS is that scaling and reliability features are often built in.

Instead of designing load balancing and server fleets manually,the platform can handle many of those tasks automatically or through simple configuration.

That reduces the number of moving parts you must manage directly.

It also reduces the chance of errors caused by complex manual infrastructure changes.

When demand increases,PaaS can handle growth in a more standardized way than hand-built servers.

This is not magic.

You still have to design your app responsibly,but it removes a lot of infrastructure complexity.

PaaS turns ops-heavy work into platform settings.

Cost in PaaS is not just about the monthly bill.

It's also about engineering time.

If PaaS allows a team to deploy faster and spend less time patching servers,that can reduce total cost even if the service pricing looks higher than raw VMs.PaaS can also reduce downtime risks caused by inconsistent server maintenance.

Another advantage is simpler onboarding.

New team members don't need to learn every detail of the infrastructure to deploy safely.

That speeds up teams and improves consistency.

The trade-off is you're paying for the platform's convenience and managed environment.

For many organizations,that trade is worth it.

PaaS is the best choice when you need to build a custom application but don't want the burden of managing servers and operating systems.It's especially good for teams that deploy frequently and want repeatable standardized deployments.

It's also useful when scaling needs to be smooth and predictable without building custom automation from scratch.

If your app fits within standard web app patterns,PaaS often delivers faster results.

If you're trying to minimize operational distractions,PaaS is a strong tool.

It's a very common choice for modern application development.

The goal is fast delivery without building every infrastructure layer manually.

A helpful way to separate PaaS and SaaS is to ask whether you're building the application or using the application.

With SaaS,you're using a finished product and your job is managing users and settings.

With PaaS,you're building and deploying your own application and the platform helps you run it.

So SAS is for consuming software while PaaS is for creating software without server babysitting.

They both reduce infrastructure work but they serve different goals.

SaaS helps end users and IT admins adopt tools quickly.

PaaS helps developers ship apps quickly.
